title: Fuel in hand
hookLine: Angiras sends the seeker to a guru with firewood in hand, and that's why students still bring an offering
carry: come to the guru with fuel in hand
last: RITES EARN A HEAVEN THAT ENDS; MOKSHA ISN'T EARNED.

lines: WHAT, ONCE KNOWN, MAKES EVERYTHING KNOWN?
cards: When you show up at someone's house for the first time, you bring something. Because it says: I came on purpose, and I'm not just here to take. The Mundaka itself opens with a visit like that.
Shaunaka, a great householder, comes to the sage Angiras the proper way and asks one question: what is it that, once known, makes everything known? Angiras's whole answer is this Upanishad.
And right after saying the rites can't carry you across, he says what can: a person, and a bundle of sticks.

teach.h: THE MADE CAN'T WIN THE UNMADE.
teach.b: Here's Angiras's verse, Mundaka 1.2.12. Having looked closely at the worlds won by works, a seeker should come to dispassion. The uncreated isn't won by the made.

teach.h: GO TO A TEACHER, FUEL IN HAND.
teach.b: To know that, let him go, fuel in hand, to a teacher who is learned in the Veda and established in Brahman. Samitpanih: samit, firewood, the sticks for the sacred fire; pani, hand. Fuel in hand.
You met this a few days ago, when the six students came to Pippalada samitpanayah, with fuel in their hands. It's the old sign of a real student: I'll serve, I'll help keep your fire going.
And notice the two qualities named for the teacher. Shrotriya: learned in the Veda, someone who has heard and studied.
And brahmanishtha: established in Brahman, someone who lives what they know. Both. Then the next verse gives the teacher a duty too.

To a student who has come properly, whose mind is calm and settled, the wise teacher should teach, truly, the knowledge by which one knows the imperishable. So the student brings fuel. The teacher brings fire.

teach.h: GURU AND SHISHYA: BOTH OWE SOMETHING.
teach.b: Both owe something. This is one of Hinduism's oldest teachings: guru and shishya, teacher and student.
The deepest knowing passes from a person who lives it, voice to ear.

It's why students of music and dance still touch a teacher's feet before a lesson, and why Guru Purnima, a full-moon day, is set aside to honor teachers. The offering isn't a fee. It says: I'm here to serve, and to learn.

how: In many Hindu traditions students approach a teacher with an offering and study in the guru-shishya relationship; Guru Purnima, on the full moon of Ashadha, is a day many set aside to honor their teachers.

o: a student who comes with fuel in hand
established in Brahman, living what they know
learned in the Veda, having heard and studied

games.q: student and teacher — tap the pairs.

s: samitpani means the student brings payment
it means fuel in hand: firewood for the teacher's sacred fire.
the Mundaka gives the teacher a duty too
to a student who comes properly, the teacher must teach truly.
the Prashna's six students also came with fuel in hand
samitpanayah: they approached Pippalada carrying firewood.

games.q: you've realized the rites can't carry you to the uncreated. what does the Mundaka tell you to do?
o: go to a teacher, fuel in hand.
games.why: go, fuel in hand, to a teacher learned in the Veda and established in Brahman. and the teacher must then teach, truly.

practice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something that mattered: a parent, a coach, an elder. Then do what many Hindus do for a teacher: fold your hands and bow to them, a pranam, here in your mind.
If bowing isn't your way, just say thank you silently. Then ask what fuel you could bring someone teaching you now: patience, attention, showing up.

wordCard.voice: Brahmanishtha, established in Brahman, one mark of a true teacher. The Mundaka's instruction: go, fuel in hand, to one who is learned in the Veda and established in Brahman, who then must teach truly.

orig.note: Sanskrit samitpāṇi: samit, firewood, + pāṇi, hand. Mundaka 1.2.12.

carryVoice: Your line: come to the guru with fuel in hand. Tomorrow, the fire that fuel was for. Day four hundred fourteen, done.

sources.ref: Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.3 (Shaunaka approaches Angiras and asks what, once known, makes everything known)
Mundaka Upanishad 1.2.12–1.2.13 (go to a teacher, fuel in hand; the teacher's duty)
